opus-5.5.text:
I think right now it's actually quite backwards: humans are the ones adapting to AI, rather than AI adapting to humans.

Look at how most people use these models today. You open a chat window and have to figure out how to phrase things. People write very long prompts and learn little tricks: "think step by step," give it a role, paste in all the context, and if the answer isn't good, rewrite the prompt and try again. There's a whole skill called prompt engineering. To me that shows the interface isn't mature yet. It's like the early days of computers, when you had to learn command lines to get anything done. The burden was on the person.

With agents it's even more obvious. When you give an agent a task, you often have to break it down very carefully, specify every constraint, and then watch it, because it might go off in a strange direction or confidently do something you didn't want. So people end up babysitting it. You're spending your own attention managing the AI, when it should be saving your attention.

From a reinforcement learning perspective, I think this is because most models are still trained to do a well-specified task well. Give it a clear math problem or a clear coding task with a verifiable reward, and it can be very strong. But real human needs are rarely well specified. When I ask a colleague for help, half of what I want is unsaid. A good collaborator asks the right clarifying question, remembers what I cared about last time, knows when to check in and when to just get it done. That kind of ability, understanding intent under ambiguity and interacting proactively, is something we haven't really trained for yet. It's harder because the reward isn't a clean right or wrong. It comes from the human, and the human is noisy and changing.

So my view is that the next important step is to flip this relationship. AI should learn to adapt to people, to understand you, to work with you over a long period of time, and to know what it doesn't know and ask. When that happens, ordinary people won't need to learn prompting at all. They'll just talk to it the way they'd talk to a capable person. I think that's what will really let AI spread to everyone, not just people who are good at "speaking AI."

r001.rationale: The response says AI should understand users’ intent and that ordinary people should not need to learn prompting, clearly indicating users would need to provide less detail.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the burden of prompting generally, but does not mention O1 or identify incorrect usage as a possible reason it is difficult to use.

fable-5.1.text:
I think right now we're in a somewhat awkward, transitional stage. People are adapting to AI more than AI is adapting to people. If you want to get good results out of a model today, you have to learn how to talk to it, how to write prompts, how to break a problem into pieces, how to check its output, and how to tell when it's confidently wrong. That's a real skill, and the people who have it get a lot more value than the people who don't. But honestly, I don't think that's how it should end up. The burden is on the wrong side.

If you look at the history of technology, early on the user always bends to the tool. With computers you had to learn command lines; with search engines, people learned to type keywords instead of sentences. Then the technology matures and the interface disappears into the background. AI is going through the same curve, just much faster. A lot of what we call "prompt engineering" now is really just compensating for the model's lack of context about you, your task, and your taste. As models get better at memory, at asking clarifying questions, at taking actions on their own, that layer of human adaptation should shrink.

That said, I don't think it goes to zero, and I don't think it should. The deeper adaptation isn't about prompting at all. It's about how people think about their own work. When a model can produce a first draft of almost anything in seconds, the valuable part of your job shifts toward judgment: knowing what to ask for, knowing what's good, knowing when to say no. From what I've seen with researchers and engineers, the ones adapting well aren't the ones memorizing tricks. They're the ones who've changed their workflow so that they spend their time on defining the problem and evaluating the answer, and let the model handle the middle. So I'd say the short-term adaptation is learning to operate the tool, and the long-term adaptation is learning what you're actually for once the tool works. The second one is harder, and we're only at the beginning of it.

r001.rationale: The response says current prompting compensates for models’ lack of context and predicts that users will need to adapt less as models improve at memory and clarifying questions.

r002.rationale: It discusses the skill needed to use models effectively, but does not connect incorrect usage to difficulty using O1.

astra-6.text:
I think people currently have to do too much of the adapting. You have to learn how to write a prompt, figure out what context the AI needs, and judge whether its answer is reliable. In a sense, you’re learning how to manage the tool before you can benefit from it.

Some learning is inevitable with any new technology. But that shouldn’t be the end goal. AI should become better at understanding what people mean, asking questions when something is unclear, and fitting into the way they already work.

For people, the most useful adjustment is learning to exercise judgment: what to delegate, what to verify, and which decisions you need to own. You shouldn’t have to become an expert in prompting just to get useful help.

r001.rationale: It says AI should better understand what people mean and ask when unclear, implying users need to provide less detail.

r002.rationale: It does not mention O1 or suggest that difficulty using it could result from incorrect usage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people currently have to do too much of the adapting. You have to learn how to phrase a request, what context to provide, and when to question the answer. Even when the system is capable, getting useful work out of it takes practice.

Some of that learning is valuable. Being clear about your goals and checking your assumptions are useful skills anyway. But I don’t think everyone should have to become an expert at prompting. AI should get better at understanding what people mean, asking questions when something is unclear, and fitting into how they already work.

For now, I’d encourage people to experiment with a task they understand well. That gives you a basis for judging where the AI helps and where it makes mistakes. You can build confidence without handing over your judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says users currently have to learn how to phrase requests and provide context, then says AI should better understand what people mean. This clearly suggests users should need to provide less detail.

r002.rationale: The response says using AI takes practice, but it does not identify incorrect usage as a reason O1 is difficult to use.
